title: Evals 101 — Doug Guthrie, Braintrust

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk is titled 'Evals 101' and centers on evaluation design, scoring methodology (LLM-as-judge, code-based scores), and the offline-to-online evaluation lifecycle. The evaluation methodology applies across AI applications generally, and the Braintrust platform is a developer tool for software builders. The session covers pre-production offline evals, production logging with online scoring, and post-production human review and user feedback. The session is explicitly an introductory '101' workshop covering fundamental evaluation concepts for newcomers. The video is described as a hands-on workshop with live platform demos and code examples. Fourteen grade-A transcript evidence anchors with specific character ranges directly support the classification.

summary: Doug Guthrie opens with a Braintrust company overview, noting CEO Anker Goyle built similar eval systems at previous companies. The agenda covers eval introduction, SDK-based eval running, production monitoring, human review, and user feedback integration. Evals answer whether application changes improve or degrade quality and detect regressions. Anker frames evals as playing offense—not just defensive unit tests—adding rigor to AI development. Connecting offline and online evals creates a flywheel effect that cuts dev time and enhances production quality. An eval has three ingredients: a task (code or prompt with input and output, from single prompt to full agentic workflow), a dataset (real-world examples with required input, optional expected output, and metadata for filtering), and scores (LLM-as-judge or code-based in TypeScript/Python, writable in-UI or from codebase). Braintrust offers an auto evals package of out-of-the-box scores. Customer tips include using higher-quality models for scoring, breaking scores into focused areas, testing score prompts in the playground, and avoiding context overload. The playground enables rapid iteration; experiments provide snapshots over time. A loop feature uses AI to optimize prompts. SDKs are available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin; users can define assets in code, push via braintrust push, and run evals via CI/CD with GitHub Actions. Moving to production requires initializing a logger, wrapping LLM clients, adding trace decorators, and creating custom spans. Online scoring applies offline-defined scores to production logs at configurable sampling rates, targeting individual spans. Regression alerts trigger when scores drop below thresholds. Human review is supported via a dedicated UI pane with configurable scores and saved filtered views. User feedback (thumbs up/down with comments) can be logged and filtered. Production logs can be added back to offline eval datasets, completing the flywheel. A Q&A covers AB testing multiple models in production (supported, with scores groupable by model), managing multiple human scorers (rubric recommended), LLM-as-judge reliability for online scoring (customers eval the judge itself), pre-launch offline evals for establishing trust (relevant for government use cases), and SDK-based export of all monitoring data to external dashboards or custom UIs. Guthrie references Sarah from Notion's workshop on human-in-the-loop organizational design, noting larger orgs use specialized PM/LLM roles while smaller orgs use engineers for review.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Braintrust SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, Kotlin) let users define prompts, scores, datasets, and full evals in code, push them to the platform, and run evals via CI/CD with GitHub Actions
Online scoring applies offline-defined scores to production logs at configurable sampling rates, optionally targeting individual spans like tool calls or RAG retrieval
The flywheel effect connects production and offline evals: production logs filtered via human review or user feedback can be added back to datasets feeding offline evals

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Doug Guthrie introduces himself as a solutions engineer at Braintrust, an end-to-end developer platform for AI products focused on evals. He outlines the agenda: company overview, intro to evals, running evals via SDK and platform, moving to production with human review and online scoring, and human-in-the-loop feedback creating a flywheel effect.

sections.title: Company Overview
sections.summary: Brief overview of Braintrust's investors and leadership, highlighting CEO Anker Goyle who built eval systems at previous companies, which inspired Braintrust's creation. Several companies already use Braintrust in production for evals and GenAI observability.

sections.title: Why Think About Evals
sections.summary: Evals help answer whether model or prompt changes improve or degrade application quality, and detect regressions. Anker described evals as a way to play offense, not just defensive unit tests, adding rigor to building non-deterministic LLM applications. Business benefits include a flywheel effect connecting production and offline evals to cut dev time and enhance quality.

sections.title: Core Concepts and What Is an Eval
sections.summary: Braintrust's core concepts include prompt engineering in a playground (IDE for LLM outputs), observability via production logs, human review, and user feedback. An eval is a structured test checking AI system performance. Three ingredients: task (code/prompt with input and output), dataset (real-world examples), and scores (LLM-as-judge or code-based heuristic/binary logic).

sections.title: Offline vs Online Evals and Getting Started
sections.summary: Offline evals are pre-production for iteration and issue resolution, defining tasks and scores. Online evals provide real-time tracing of production inputs, outputs, intermediate steps, and tool calls, with metrics on cost, tokens, and duration. Advice: just get started and build a baseline. A diagnostic matrix guides targeting efforts based on output quality and score alignment.

sections.title: Platform Demo: Task Components
sections.summary: Demonstrates task creation in the Braintrust platform: selecting a model, writing system prompts, using mustache templating for variables, adding multi-turn messages, attaching tools (RAG, web search), and a beta agentic workflow feature for chaining prompts where one output becomes the next input.

sections.title: Datasets, Scores, and Auto Evals Package
sections.summary: Covers datasets in detail: required input, optional expected output (enabling scores like Levenshtein for measuring difference), and metadata for filtering. Scores include code-based (TypeScript/Python in-UI or from codebase) and LLM-as-judge with custom criteria. Introduces the auto evals package of out-of-the-box scores. Stresses starting small and iterating. Human review of production logs can feed datasets for offline evals.

sections.title: Customer Tips for Scoring
sections.summary: Customer-derived tips: use higher-quality models for scoring even if the application uses cheaper ones; break scoring into focused targeted areas (separate accuracy, formatting, correctness rather than one combined score); test score prompts in the playground before use; and avoid overloading the score or prompt with context, focusing on relevant input and output.

sections.title: Playground and Experiments Overview
sections.summary: The playground enables rapid iteration combining prompts, agents, datasets, and scores with a run button. Developers, PMs, and even doctors at a healthcare company use it. Experiments provide snapshots in time to track whether changes improve performance over periods like months. Evals can run from the platform or via SDK.

sections.title: Demo: Changelog App and Model Comparison
sections.summary: Live demo of a changelog-generation app taking a GitHub repo URL, fetching commits, producing a changelog, and accepting user feedback. Shows loading prompts from codebase into the platform, duplicating prompts to compare models (e.g., GPT-41), adding datasets and scores, running evals in parallel, and viewing the summary layout comparing base vs comparison task across completeness, accuracy, and formatting scores.

sections.title: Demo: Loop Feature and Experiments
sections.summary: Demonstrates a new loop feature (released same day) that uses AI to optimize prompts in a Cursor-like interface, accessing eval results to determine if changes improve scores. Shows the diff and acceptance flow (though an Anthropic API key issue prevented full execution). Also shows running experiments as snapshots to track performance over time. Concludes by summarizing eval ingredients and transitioning to SDK usage.

sections.title: SDK Usage: Defining and Pushing Eval Components from Code
sections.summary: Braintrust offers Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin SDKs, with most users on Python or TypeScript. Guthrie shows code examples of defining prompts, scores, and datasets within a codebase and pushing them to Braintrust via a braintrust push command. These assets become version-controlled in the platform. He also shows defining full evals in code using an Eval class that references a dataset, task, and scores, then running the eval and viewing it as an experiment in the platform. This supports two workflow types: defining assets in code or in the UI, catering to different organizational preferences.

sections.title: SDK Evals and CI/CD Integration
sections.summary: Guthrie recaps the SDK workflow and highlights key motivations: source-controlling prompts, and enabling online scoring by pushing scores into Braintrust so production performance can be measured against offline eval scores. He notes evals can be run via CI/CD pipelines, with some customers using evals as automated quality checks in CI. Braintrust documentation includes a GitHub Actions example for setup.

sections.title: Moving to Production: Logging and Instrumentation
sections.summary: Moving to production requires instrumenting applications with Braintrust logging code. Key motivations include measuring quality on live traffic with the same scores used offline, and creating the flywheel effect by adding production logs back to datasets. Setup begins with initializing a logger to authenticate and point to a project (a container for a feature's prompts, scores, and datasets). Users can start simply by wrapping an LLM client for automatic token, duration, and cost metrics, then add trace decorators to functions and create custom spans with specified inputs, outputs, and metadata for more granular logging.

sections.title: Online Scoring, Regression Alerts, and Custom Views
sections.summary: Online scoring allows configuring scores to run on incoming production logs at a sampling rate (e.g., 10%, 20%, 100%), creating a tight feedback loop. Scores can be applied to individual spans (e.g., tool calls, RAG retrieval) rather than just the root span. Regression alerts can trigger automations when scores drop below thresholds. Custom views with filters help humans parse through logs for review, focusing on the most meaningful entries.

sections.title: Demo: Production Logging, Online Scoring, and User Feedback
sections.summary: Guthrie shows code wrapping a Vercel AI SDK model for automatic Braintrust logging with zero developer lift, and defining custom spans with specific inputs and outputs to ensure consistency with offline datasets. He demonstrates configuring online scoring in the platform by creating a rule, selecting scores, setting a 100% sampling rate, and applying scores to individual spans. Running the changelog app again shows scores appearing in production logs. He also demonstrates user feedback (thumbs up/down with comments) logged to Braintrust, visible as a user feedback score, and filtering logs by user feedback equals zero to surface problematic cases for human review.

sections.title: Human Review UI and Granular Span Scoring
sections.summary: Guthrie demonstrates saving filtered views for human review (e.g., user feedback equals zero) and shows the human review pane (opened via button or R key) with a pared-down log view and configurable human review scores. He highlights granular tracing of tool calls in the changelog app (fetching GitHub commits and latest release). He then shows a conversational analytics application where individual spans are scored—e.g., question rephrasing quality and intent derivation—demonstrating the value of span-level scoring both offline and online for complex multi-step applications.

sections.title: Human-in-the-Loop Discussion and Notion Reference
sections.summary: Guthrie references Sarah from Notion's Tuesday workshop on human-in-the-loop organizational design: larger organizations use a specialized role combining PM and LLM specialist for human review, while smaller organizations have engineers do the review. He emphasizes pairing automation with human review adds lasting value. Two types of human-in-the-loop are summarized: human review (in-platform interface with configurable scores) and user feedback (from application users, powering views and the flywheel). He stresses this is critical for application quality, reliability, and providing ground truth.

sections.title: Q&A: Flywheel, AB Testing, and Multiple Scorers
sections.summary: Audience Q&A begins. Guthrie demonstrates adding production log rows back to offline eval datasets to complete the flywheel. On AB testing multiple models in production, he confirms support and shows scores grouped by underlying model. On managing multiple human scorers with different criteria, he recommends establishing a rubric or guideline; the platform shows who scored what, though pulling inter-scorer differences as a dataset is not currently a feature.

sections.title: Q&A: LLM-as-Judge, Pre-Launch Evals, and SDK Export
sections.summary: On LLM-as-judge relativistic vs absolute scores for online use, Guthrie notes customers can eval the judge itself via its rationale, referencing Sarah from Notion's described process. A government-sector questioner asks about pre-launch evals; Guthrie clarifies these are offline evals used to establish baselines and build stakeholder trust before production. On exporting monitoring data to external dashboards, he confirms all data (experiments, datasets, logs) is available via SDK, and one customer built a custom UI on top of the SDK. The session concludes with applause.
